::: {style="margin-top: 1em; font-size: 125%; font-weight: 1000; text-align: center;"}
Average of what?
:::

<!-- ## Concepts and intuitions {.unnumbered} -->

What is the average age of Malagasy population?
What is the average age of men in Madagascar?
What is the average age of men in Melaky region?

Above are three examples of calculating the average age but based on three different "population". It should be clear that unless you specify the second part of the question (which we call population) that question is pointless. The answer then depend on which population is under study.

As one can argue, the first part of the question is more important, and more interesting. For instance the crucial difference between a difference and differential equation (@sec-difference and @sec-differential) is that the is @sec-discrete_continuous. Since the starting set is skipped, hence the existence of this chapter.

One could also argue that it is the second part (i.e. the characterisation of the population) that is more interesting. Indeed, when asking people what research they are doing, they answer, I study lemurs in Ranomfana, grasslands or ants. Most of the time, these answers are also not precise enough. The one is to think/define/delimit more precisely about one means by population.

Convince oneself, one is not more important than the other,  no need to set an order of piority and embrace the complementarity.

Beyond the rather philosophical aspect, the practical side is we almost never know the population. For the three examples of population above: no one will every collect data on age of every individuals in the population. So in principle we will never know the answers to these questions. And this is the disctintion between a population and a sample, and the difference between a true value and the estimated value. The disctinction is important enough they are distinguised by notation: the true value is represented by greek letter, while the estimated by roman letters.

## Formal {.unnumbered}

Textbook Source
Book: Introduction to the Theory of Statistics (3rd Edition)
Authors: Alexander M. Mood, Franklin A. Graybill, and Duane C. Boes
Publisher: McGraw-Hill

The Definition
Mood, Graybill, and Boes provide a highly rigorous, set-theoretic approach to defining a statistical population:

"A population is a collection of items (or measurements of items) under study...There are two rigorous sub-definitions:
First the existent (or Tangible) Population: A concrete, finite set of existing elements, denoted by a finite index set P={1,2,…,N} (discrete: @sec-discrete_continuous). In this handbook (there are other definitions), we consider the population as the whole set and not a result of a sampling.

Second the hypothetical Population: An infinite set of all possible outcomes that could be generated by a repeatable experiment (e.g., an infinite sequence of coin tosses), which is mathematically represented entirely by its probability law, P(⋅). While introduced for completness, we will return to this later, mostly because it involves probability which is by order its not assumed to be understood.

## Tips and warnings {.unnumbered}
- To reiterate, a population is well-defined collection of items. Knowing what is included and not included in the population is critical/ delimitation is non-trivial. Say Malagasy population: does it include people living in Madagascar (immigrants), people with, so do we exclude those in the countryside that might not a have a birth certificate? How about Malagasy living abroad?
-  Defining the items can be non-trivial. It could be simple for animals.  For instance, for grasses, what is a population? Di we care about individual ants or colony Eusocial? This is what is an item.
- @sec-sec-function, is defined by set if X and Y, pop is the starting set don't ignore it.
- Unless you sample everything, one cannot  see the rare nitpick example above. Statistical inference: estimate the true population vs sample?
- Population itself is not the end goal, it is studing the properties of that population (variables @sec-sec-variable, distribution @sec-distribution).
- Population is a sample. While in more rigorous, foundational, the more practical is more useful for the applied scientist.
